title: Net Thirty #58: The three-line late payment email
content:
From: Net Thirty <hello@netthirty.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-01T13:05:02Z

NET THIRTY
Money notes for people who invoice for a living
Issue 58

Good morning,

Most late payments are not refusals. They are an invoice sitting in somebody's inbox under forty other things. This issue is about making the follow-up so easy to act on that nobody has to think.

1. THE THREE-LINE FOLLOW-UP

Day 1 after the due date:
"Hi Jordan, invoice 1043 came due yesterday. Here is the payment link again in case it got buried. Thanks!"

Day 7:
"Hi Jordan, checking in on invoice 1043, now a week past due. If something on our side is blocking payment (a PO number, a vendor form, a different billing contact), tell me and I will fix it today."

Day 14:
"Hi Jordan, invoice 1043 is two weeks past due. Can you tell me the date it will be paid? I will pause new work until I have a date."

Notice the pattern. Each message names the invoice, names one next step, and offers a way out that is not a confrontation. Readers who switched to this sequence told us roughly a third of their "late" invoices were paid within a day of the first message.

2. READER QUESTION

"One client pays all vendors in a single batch on the 20th. Should I time my invoices to land just before it?"

Yes. Ask their accounts payable contact for the batch calendar once, then put the cutoff in your own calendar. A twelve-minute email now saves a month of waiting every time you miss the window by a day.

3. WORTH YOUR TIME

- Why we stopped saying "net 30" in proposals and started writing an actual date: https://netthirty.example/notes/write-the-date
- A one-page late fee clause in plain English: https://netthirty.example/templates/late-fee
- Interview: a bookkeeper on what she wishes freelancers put on invoices: https://netthirty.example/interviews/bookkeeper-checklist

Until the 15th,
Carmen

--

title: Fix Astro build failing on image import
content:
Claude Code session in /Users/jules/code/marlowworks-site (main)

USER: ci build is red again but npm run build is fine on my laptop. says rollup failed to resolve an image import. can you dig in

ASSISTANT: I'll start with what CI reported and then try to reproduce it. A build that passes on a Mac and fails on a Linux runner over a missing file is very often a casing problem. The default macOS filesystem ignores case and Linux does not, so I'll check that first.

TOOL Bash: gh run list --limit 3

RESULT: completed	failure	Add case study template	build	main	push	11849203314	41s	about 12 minutes ago
completed	success	Fix footer links	build	main	push	11846120877	58s	about 3 hours ago
completed	success	Bump astro	build	main	push	11839904102	1m2s	about 1 day ago

TOOL Bash: gh run view 11849203314 --log-failed | rg -n "error|Rollup|resolve" | head

RESULT: 31:build	Build site	2026-09-01T15:09:41.7120043Z [vite]: Rollup failed to resolve import "../assets/hero.png" from "/actions-runner/_work/marlowworks-site/marlowworks-site/src/pages/index.astro".
32:build	Build site	2026-09-01T15:09:41.7121290Z This is most likely unintended because it can break you …

TOOL Grep: hero\.png in /Users/jules/code/marlowworks-site/src

RESULT: src/pages/index.astro:3:import hero from '../assets/hero.png';
src/components/CaseStudyCard.astro:4:import fallback from '../assets/hero.png';

ASSISTANT: The import is lowercase `hero.png` in two places. Now the question is what git thinks the file is called, since that is what the runner checks out.

TOOL Bash: ls src/assets && echo --- && git ls-files src/assets

RESULT: Hero.png
blog
logo.svg
---
src/assets/Hero.png
src/assets/blog/what-i-check-before-automating.jpg
src/assets/logo.svg

ASSISTANT: That is the cause. On disk the file is `Hero.png`, and git also tracks `Hero.png`, but the code imports `hero.png`. macOS resolves the lowercase import to the capitalized file, so it works here. The Linux runner finds no `hero.png` and the build stops.

There are two ways out. I could change both imports to `Hero.png`, which is quick but leaves a capitalized filename that will trip someone again. Or I could rename the file to lowercase so it matches every other asset. I'd rename it, because the rest of `src/assets` is lowercase. Renaming only the case of a file needs two steps with git on a case-insensitive filesystem, otherwise git sees no change.

USER: rename it, lowercase everywhere

TOOL Bash: git mv src/assets/Hero.png src/assets/hero-tmp.png && git mv src/assets/hero-tmp.png src/assets/hero.png && git ls-files src/assets

RESULT: src/assets/blog/what-i-check-before-automating.jpg
src/assets/hero.png
src/assets/logo.svg

ASSISTANT: Git now tracks `hero.png`. While I'm here I'll look for other imports with a casing mismatch, since one is likely not the only one. I'll compare every asset import against the tracked file list, ignoring case.

TOOL Bash: rg -o --no-filename "(?:import|from) .*['\"](\.\./)+assets/[^'\"]+['\"]" src | rg -o "assets/[^'\"]+" | sort -u

RESULT: assets/blog/what-i-check-before-automating.jpg
assets/hero.png
assets/logo.svg

TOOL Bash: for f in $(rg -o --no-filename "assets/[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+\.(png|jpg|svg)" src | sort -u); do git ls-files --error-unmatch "src/$f" >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "NOT TRACKED AS WRITTEN: $f"; done

RESULT: (no output)

ASSISTANT: Every asset path written in `src` now matches a tracked file exactly. Frontmatter image paths in the blog content are checked by the collection schema at build time, so the build covers those. I'll run the production build, then a case-sensitive check the way CI sees it.

TOOL Bash: npm run build 2>&1 | tail -12

RESULT: 15:31:07 [build] 14 page(s) built in 6.84s
15:31:07 [build] Complete!

ASSISTANT: That passes, but it passed before too, so it proves nothing about the Linux case. To test the same condition as the runner, I'll clone the repo into a fresh directory from my working tree and build there. Git checks out files by their tracked names, so the clone shows what CI will see.

TOOL Bash: git add -A && git commit -qm "Rename hero image to lowercase so Linux builds resolve it" && git clone -q . /tmp/site-ci-check && cd /tmp/site-ci-check && ls src/assets && npm ci --silent && npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4

RESULT: blog
hero.png
logo.svg
15:36:52 [build] 14 page(s) built in 6.51s
15:36:52 [build] Complete!

ASSISTANT: A fresh checkout now has `hero.png` and builds. I looked at whether to add a guard so this cannot happen again. Git's `core.ignorecase` setting does not help, because it only changes how git compares names, not how macOS opens files. A CI step that fails on mixed-case asset names would work, but with one offender in the whole tree it is more machinery than the problem earns. I'm leaving it at the rename.

USER: ok fine, just push it

TOOL Bash: git push origin main && rm -rf /tmp/site-ci-check

RESULT: To github.com:marlow-works/marlowworks-site.git
   3e1f9a2..b7c40de  main -> main

TOOL Bash: gh run watch --exit-status 2>&1 | tail -6

RESULT: Refreshing run status every 3 seconds. Press Ctrl+C to quit.
✓ main build · 11849877120
Triggered via push less than a minute ago
✓ build in 54s

ASSISTANT: CI is green on the new commit.

**Cause.** The image was `Hero.png` on disk and in git, and two files imported `hero.png`. macOS ignored the casing difference, the Linux runner did not.

**Fix.** I renamed the file to `hero.png` in two steps with `git mv` through a temporary name, because a direct case-only rename is a no-op on a case-insensitive filesystem. Both imports already used the lowercase name, so no code changed.

**Checked.** A fresh clone builds with 14 pages, and the CI run after the push finished green. I did not add a CI guard for casing, since renaming the one file removed the only mismatch I found.

title: [default/telegram] Crispy roasted chickpeas
content:
Hermes telegram session, profile default, Jules Marlow

USER: how do i get roasted chickpeas actually crispy, mine always come out chewy

TOOL web_search: crispy roasted chickpeas oven temperature dry method

RESULT: Dry them thoroughly after draining, roast at 425F (220C) for 25-30 minutes, shake the pan halfway. Season after roasting if using fine spices because they scorch. Let them cool in the oven with the do …

ASSISTANT: Chewy usually means moisture. What works:

1. Drain and rinse, then dry them properly. Spread on a towel and rub, and let them air dry another 10 minutes. Loose skins can come off.
2. Toss with about a tablespoon of oil per can and salt. Not much more or they steam.
3. Roast on a single layer at 425F (220C) for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the pan halfway.
4. Turn the oven off and leave them inside with the door cracked for 10 minutes. That last step is what firms them up.

Add paprika or cumin right after they come out. Fine spices burn if they go in at the start.

USER: ok trying that tonight

ASSISTANT: Good luck. If they are still soft, the pan was probably crowded, so use two pans next time.

title: Quiet Workflow 212: Three ways orders reach a spreadsheet
content:
From: Quiet Workflow <weekly@quietworkflow.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-02T12:30:05Z

QUIET WORKFLOW
Issue 212 | Automation for small teams without an IT department

Hi,

Four people wrote in this week with the same question: "Orders come in from three places and I type them into a spreadsheet. Now what?" So let's walk through it.

THREE WAYS ORDERS REACH A SPREADSHEET

1. A form that writes to Google Sheets. Boring, reliable, and the right answer more often than people want to admit. If you can send customers to a form, do that first.

2. Email parsing. Forward order emails to a mailbox a script reads, pull out the fields, append a row. Works when the senders are other businesses writing in a consistent template. Falls apart with humans.

3. Text messages or DMs. Customers love them and they are the messiest input. You get "two dozen of the usual, pick up sat" with no name attached. This is where people reach for a language model, and where you need a confirmation step (more on that in issue 215).

THE ONE THAT FAILS

Copy and paste by a person at the end of a long day. It works until the week somebody is out sick and the sheet is three days behind. If a human is the integration, schedule a replacement for the human.

CASE FILE: A GROOMING SALON IN TULSA

Waggle Grooming took bookings by phone, text and web form, and the receptionist copied everything into one calendar sheet. Before automating anything they added a "source" column and a "raw message" column. When a booking looked wrong, they could see exactly what the customer had written. Debugging time dropped, and so did the arguments.

TOOL OF THE WEEK

Apps Script time-driven triggers. A few lines of script, run every five minutes, can tidy new rows (trim whitespace, normalize phone numbers) without any extra service. Walkthrough: https://quietworkflow.example/tools/apps-script-triggers

Reply to this email if you have a workflow you'd like us to dissect.
Tobias

title: The Recall Letter #77: No-shows by day of week, and what 140 practices reported
content:
From: The Recall Letter <hello@recallletter.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-02T13:40:17Z

THE RECALL LETTER
Front-desk and practice management notes for dental offices | Issue 77

NO-SHOWS BY DAY OF WEEK: WHAT 140 PRACTICES REPORTED

Our spring survey asked practices to export 90 days of appointments and send back four numbers: scheduled, kept, cancelled, no-show. 140 practices replied. The median no-show rate was 6.1 percent, with a range from under 2 to over 15.

The weekday pattern was less dramatic than office folklore suggests. Mondays were worst at 7.4 percent, Thursdays best at 4.9. The bigger spread was by visit type. New patient visits were missed at roughly double the rate of recall cleanings.

WHAT CEDAR ROW DENTAL CHANGED

Cedar Row Dental, a four-chair practice in Columbus, Ohio, moved from a phone call two days out to a text with a one-tap confirm link. Office manager Lena Fisk told us: "The calls got answered about a third of the time. The texts get answered inside the hour." Their no-show rate went from 8.2 to 5.5 percent over two quarters with the same staff.

Her two caveats. One: texts to landline numbers fail silently, so they still call anyone whose number comes back flagged. Two: patients who reply with a question ("can I come at 3 instead?") need a person to see the reply the same day, or the text feels worse than a voicemail.

SCRIPT SWAP

Old: "This is a reminder that you have an appointment on Thursday. Please call if you cannot make it."
New: "Hi Maria, it's Cedar Row Dental. We have you down for Thursday afternoon. Tap here to confirm or pick a new time: [link]"

The second one asks for something specific and makes the easy answer one tap long.

WORTH A CLICK

- The full survey tables (members): https://recallletter.example/survey/spring
- A cancellation policy you can adapt: https://recallletter.example/templates/cancellation-policy
- Webinar replay, filling same-day openings from a waitlist: https://recallletter.example/webinars/waitlist

Until the 16th,
The Recall Letter team

title: [default/telegram] Cups of bread flour to grams
content:
Hermes telegram session, profile default, Jules Marlow

USER: recipe says 3 1/2 cups bread flour, i have a scale. how many grams

ASSISTANT: About 420 g. The usual figure for bread flour is 120 g per cup, so 3 1/2 cups is 3.5 x 120 = 420 g.

If you scoop straight from the bag a cup can weigh 140 to 150 g because the flour packs down, which would make the dough too dry. Going by the scale at 420 g is safer than counting cups.

USER: and if it were all purpose

ASSISTANT: Same 120 g per cup, so also about 420 g. Bread flour has more protein, so the dough will feel a bit stronger and take a little more water, but the weight per cup is close enough that the conversion does not change.

title: Walrus Digest #301: fixtures you overuse, uv in CI, table extraction
content:
From: Walrus Digest <editor@walrusdigest.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-03T13:00:02Z

WALRUS DIGEST
Issue 301 | A weekly roundup for people who write Python for a living

Morning,

Short issue this week. Three things worth your coffee.

1. FIXTURES YOU'RE OVERUSING

A pytest fixture that does five things is a hidden dependency. The piece by Maren Haugen makes the case for small fixtures that each build one object, composed explicitly in the test. Her rule of thumb: if you have to open conftest.py to understand a test, the fixture has too much in it. https://walrusdigest.example/links/small-fixtures

2. UV IN CI, ONE YEAR LATER

A team of eleven moved their pipelines from pip to uv and wrote up the numbers: cold install went from about 90 seconds to under 10, and cache hit rates stopped being a coin flip. The surprise was lock file diffs in code review. They became readable, so people actually read them. https://walrusdigest.example/links/uv-in-ci

3. PULLING TABLES OUT OF PDFS WITH PDFPLUMBER

A tutorial that goes past the README. It covers the difference between lines-based and text-based table strategies, how to crop to a region before extracting, and why you should print `page.extract_words()` before you decide anything is broken. The author processes carrier-style invoices and has a nice trick for stitching a table that wraps across pages. https://walrusdigest.example/links/pdfplumber-tables

QUICK LINKS

- Pydantic models at API boundaries, dataclasses inside: https://walrusdigest.example/links/models-at-boundaries
- A tiny CLI for diffing two CSVs by key: https://walrusdigest.example/links/csvdiff
- "I deleted my mocks and my tests got better": https://walrusdigest.example/links/fewer-mocks

ONE OPINION

If your project has a `utils.py` over 300 lines, it has a missing module in it. Name the thing.

Next week: FastAPI background tasks versus a real queue.

Until Thursday,
The Walrus Digest team

ASSISTANT: Each package directory mirrors the home directory, so stow can link `zsh/.zshrc` to `~/.zshrc` directly. The system bash is 3.2, which is old: no associative arrays, no `mapfile`, and an empty array counts as unset under `set -u`. Then run `stow --restow` for each package, which is safe to repeat. And with `--dry-run`, print what would be moved and run `stow -n`, changing nothing. title: The Backhaul: Spot rates soften as peak season stalls
content:
From: The Backhaul <desk@backhaulbrief.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-04T12:00:24Z

THE BACKHAUL
Vol. 9, No. 33 | Freight and logistics news, Fridays

SPOT RATES SOFTEN AS PEAK SEASON STALLS

National dry van spot rates averaged $2.04 per mile this week, down three cents from the week before, according to the broker index we track. Reefer held roughly flat at $2.46. Flatbed was the outlier, up a nickel on construction demand in the Mountain West.

Brokers told us the usual early-fall surge is running late. Retail import volume is still arriving, but shippers are spacing out pickups instead of dumping them into one week. "It's a drip, not a flood," one Midwest broker said.

DETENTION: WHO GETS PAID, AND HOW

A survey of 400 carriers found 62 percent billed detention at least once last quarter, but only 38 percent were paid in full. The most common reason for a short pay was not the dwell time itself but missing timestamps. Carriers whose drivers photographed the check-in sheet and kept the bill of lading stamped with in and out times collected far more often.

Takeaway for small carriers: the paperwork is the claim. If the in-time is not on a document, the invoice will be negotiated.

PAPERWORK WATCH

Invoice mismatches remain the top reason for slow payment between carriers and shippers. The usual suspects are a rate confirmation that says one thing and an invoice that says another, a fuel surcharge figured on the wrong week's index, and lumper receipts that never made it into the packet. Several mid-size shippers now reject invoices automatically when the load number on the PDF does not match their TMS.

Meanwhile, more carriers are trying OCR to read invoices and bills of lading. Accuracy on clean scans is above 95 percent in vendor demos. On documents that were faxed and then scanned, nobody wants to quote a number.

IN BRIEF

- Tamarack Line Haul named a new CFO after eight months with the seat empty.
- The port at Savannah reported its busiest August on record.
- Redfern Freight is acquiring Alder & Cole Logistics, terms undisclosed.

That is the week. Forward this to a dispatcher you like.
The Backhaul desk

title: Traceback trimming regex does nothing on Python 3.11 and newer
content:
Claude Code session in /Users/jules/code/pinch (fix/py311-tracebacks)

USER: someone pasted me a traceback from python 3.12 and pinch didn't trim it at all, the whole thing came out untouched. 3.9 tracebacks work fine. find out why

ASSISTANT: Tracebacks changed in 3.11. Frames can now carry an extra line of `~~~^^^` markers under the source line. My guess is the regex assumes exactly one source line per frame, so a frame with a marker line breaks the match. I'll confirm that before touching anything. First the current pattern.

TOOL Read: /Users/jules/code/pinch/pinch/trim.py

RESULT: import re

TRACEBACK = re.compile(
    r"Traceback \(most recent call last\):\n"
    r"(?P<frames>(?:  File \".*\", line \d+, in .*\n(?:    .*\n)?)+)"
    r"(?P<error>\S.*)"
)

ASSISTANT: Each frame is a `File` line plus at most one more line, written `(?:    .*\n)?`. A 3.12 frame with a marker line has two. To reproduce it I need a real traceback long enough that trimming should happen, since a short one is left alone on purpose. I'll make a recursive function and capture the interpreter's own output.

TOOL Bash: mkdir -p /tmp/tb && cat > /tmp/tb/gen.py <<'EOF'
def a(n):
    return b(n) + 1
def b(n):
    return c(n) * 2
def c(n):
    if n == 0:
        return {}["x"]
    return a(n - 1)
a(3)
EOF
uv run python --version; uv run python /tmp/tb/gen.py 2> /tmp/tb/long312.txt; wc -l < /tmp/tb/long312.txt; sed -n  …

RESULT: Python 3.12.7
40
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/tmp/tb/gen.py", line 9, in <module>
    a(3)
  File "/tmp/tb/gen.py", line 2, in a
    return b(n) + 1
           ^^^^^^
  File "/tmp/tb/gen.py", line 4, in b
    return c(n) * 2

TOOL Bash: uv run pinch /tmp/tb/long312.txt | wc -l; uv run python - <<'EOF'
from pinch.trim import TRACEBACK
text = open("/tmp/tb/long312.txt").read()
print("matches:", bool(TRACEBACK.search(text)))
EOF

RESULT: 40
matches: False

ASSISTANT: That reproduces it. The real traceback has 40 lines, pinch printed 40 lines, and the pattern does not match at all. That fits the guess. After the first marker line the repeat cannot continue, the `error` group needs a non-space character, the marker line starts with spaces, and the whole pattern fails. Nothing is trimmed.

The fix is to allow any number of indented lines per frame. Lines that belong to a frame are indented four spaces and the `File` lines two, so `(?:    .*\n)*` is unambiguous. I'll pull the frame pattern out into a named constant, since the code that splits frames also needs it. Let me read that code first.

ASSISTANT: Committed, not pushed.

**Cause.** The `TRACEBACK` pattern allowed one source line per frame. Python 3.11 added marker lines under the source line, so a frame has two indented lines, the match failed on the first marker, and nothing was trimmed.

**Fix.** One `FRAME` pattern in `pinch/trim.py` that allows any number of four-space lines after each `File` line, used both by the matcher and by the code that splits frames. My first edit referred to `FRAME` before it was defined and failed on import, so I moved it above `TRACEBACK`.

**Checked.** A real 3.12 traceback of 13 frames now trims to four frames with a marker saying nine are hidden, and a 3.9 style traceback still trims as before. A parametrized test covers both formats, and it fails on the old pattern for the 3.12 case. Not covered: chained exceptions (`During handling of the above exception...`), which I did not try.

title: [default/telegram] Regression to the mean explained
content:
Hermes telegram session, profile default, Jules Marlow

USER: a podcast keeps saying regression to the mean and i nod along but dont really get it

ASSISTANT: It means extreme results tend to be followed by less extreme ones, even when nothing changed except luck.

Example: you bowl a score far above your usual average. Part of that was skill and part was a lucky day. The next game the luck is unlikely to repeat, so you probably score closer to your average. Nothing about you got worse.

It matters because people see the swing back and invent a cause. A team that wins the coach of the month award has a worse month after. The award did not jinx it. The great month was partly luck, and luck does not carry over.

A quick check: if a result was far from normal and the next one moves back toward normal, ask whether you need a cause at all.

USER: ok that actually makes sense

title: Speed up zsh startup time
content:
Claude Code session in /Users/jules/code/dotfiles (main)

USER: my terminal takes over half a second to show a prompt. profile .zshrc and fix whatever is slow

ASSISTANT: I'll measure first so I know what the number is and which part of the file causes it. `hyperfine` runs the shell many times and gives a mean, and `zprof` shows where the time goes inside one startup.

TOOL Bash: hyperfine --warmup 3 'zsh -i -c exit' 2>&1 | head -6

RESULT: Benchmark 1: zsh -i -c exit
  Time (mean ± σ):     642.3 ms ±   8.1 ms    [User: 361.2 ms, System: 247.9 ms]
  Range (min … max):   629.8 ms … 655.0 ms    10 runs

TOOL Read: /Users/jules/code/dotfiles/zsh/.zshrc

RESULT: export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"
[ -s "/opt/homebrew/opt/nvm/nvm.sh" ] && \. "/opt/homebrew/opt/nvm/nvm.sh"

eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
eval "$(starship init zsh)"
source <(fzf --zsh)

autoload -Uz compinit && compinit

ASSISTANT: Four candidates here: sourcing `nvm.sh`, `brew shellenv`, `starship init`, and an uncached `compinit`. I suspect `nvm.sh` most, since it is known to be slow, but I'll check with the profiler and not assume. I'll load `zprof` at the top of a copy of the file so I don't change your real one.

TOOL Bash: cp zsh/.zshrc /tmp/zshrc-prof && sed -i '' '1i\
zmodload zsh/zprof' /tmp/zshrc-prof && echo 'zprof | head -14' >> /tmp/zshrc-prof && mkdir -p /tmp/zdot && cp /tmp/zshrc-prof /tmp/zdot/.zshrc && ZDOTDIR=/tmp/zdot zsh -i -c exit

RESULT: num  calls                time                       self            name
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 1)    1         318.77   318.77   50.20%    318.77   318.77   50.20%  nvm_auto
 2)    1         141.02   141.02   22.21%    141.02   141.02   …

ASSISTANT: The suspicion holds. `nvm` accounts for about half the startup (319 ms), `compinit` for about a fifth (141 ms) and `brew shellenv` for around 50 ms. `starship` is about 24 ms, which I'll leave because it is the prompt itself.

Three fixes, each small:

1. **Lazy-load nvm.** Define stub functions named `nvm`, `node`, `npm` and `npx`. The first time you run any of them the stub removes itself, loads the real `nvm.sh` and runs your command. Shell startup pays nothing, and the first `node` call in a session pays about 300 ms once.
2. **Cache the completion dump.** `compinit` rebuilds its dump and checks every completion file on each start. `compinit -C` skips that check. I'll run the full check only if the dump is more than 24 hours old.
3. **Replace `brew shellenv` with fixed exports.** Its output never changes on this machine, so spawning a process every time is wasteful.

TOOL Bash: /opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv

RESULT: export HOMEBREW_PREFIX="/opt/homebrew";
export HOMEBREW_CELLAR="/opt/homebrew/Cellar";
export HOMEBREW_REPOSITORY="/opt/homebrew";
fpath[1,0]="/opt/homebrew/share/zsh/site-functions";
eval "$(/usr/bin/env PATH_HELPER_ROOT="/opt/homebrew" /usr/libexec/path_helper -s)"
[ -z "${MANPATH-}" ] || export M …

ASSISTANT: It also runs `path_helper`, which is the slow part, and rewrites `fpath`. I need the `fpath` line, because completions for brew-installed tools depend on it, and the PATH entries. I'll write the equivalent by hand and keep `fpath` correct, since losing it would silently break tab completion for tools like `gh` and `uv`.

TOOL Edit: /Users/jules/code/dotfiles/zsh/.zshrc
old: export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"
[ -s "/opt/homebrew/opt/nvm/nvm.sh" ] && \. "/opt/homebrew/opt/nvm/nvm.sh"

eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
new: export HOMEBREW_PREFIX="/opt/homebrew"
export HOMEBREW_CELLAR="$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/Cellar"
export PATH="$HOME …

RESULT: The file /Users/jules/code/dotfiles/zsh/.zshrc has been updated.

TOOL Edit: /Users/jules/code/dotfiles/zsh/.zshrc
old: autoload -Uz compinit && compinit
new: autoload -Uz compinit
if [[ -n ${ZDOTDIR:-$HOME}/.zcompdump(#qN.mh+24) ]]; then
  compinit
else
  compinit -C
fi

RESULT: The file /Users/jules/code/dotfiles/zsh/.zshrc has been updated.

ASSISTANT: The glob `(#qN.mh+24)` matches the dump file only if it is a regular file modified more than 24 hours ago, and `N` keeps it from erroring when the file does not exist. Let me time it and check that nothing broke.

TOOL Bash: hyperfine --warmup 3 'zsh -i -c exit' 2>&1 | sed -n 2,3p

RESULT: Time (mean ± σ):      97.6 ms ±   2.3 ms    [User: 52.1 ms, System: 38.9 ms]
  Range (min … max):    94.4 ms … 101.8 ms    10 runs

ASSISTANT: From 642 ms to 98 ms. A faster shell that cannot find its tools is worse than a slow one, though, so I'll check four things: PATH order, the `fpath` entry, the lazy functions, and that `node` loads on first use.

TOOL Bash: zsh -i -c 'echo "$PATH" | tr ":" "\n" | head -3; echo ---; print -l $fpath | head -2; echo ---; whence -w nvm node npm npx'

ASSISTANT: The first call to `node` loads nvm, afterwards `whence` reports `node` as a file, and the second call is just the binary. Everything is where it should be. One more thing to test is completions, since `compinit -C` can serve a stale dump. I'll check that a completion function from a brew package is registered.

TOOL Bash: zsh -i -c 'print -r -- ${_comps[gh]:-MISSING} ${_comps[uv]:-MISSING} ${_comps[git]:-MISSING}'

RESULT: _gh _uv _git

ASSISTANT: Completions for `gh`, `uv` and `git` are registered. The 24 hour rule means a newly installed tool's completions can take up to a day to appear. If that bites, deleting `~/.zcompdump` forces a rebuild on the next shell. I'll put that into a comment in the file, since the behavior is not obvious from the code.

TOOL Edit: /Users/jules/code/dotfiles/zsh/.zshrc

RESULT: 7be40a2 zsh: lazy-load nvm, cache compinit, drop brew shellenv from startup

ASSISTANT: Committed locally.

**Result.** Startup went from 642 ms to 98 ms on `hyperfine` with 10 runs each, for `zsh -i -c exit`.

**What was slow.** The profiler showed `nvm.sh` at 319 ms, `compinit` at 141 ms and `brew shellenv` at about 52 ms. Together they were about four fifths of the time.

**What changed in `zsh/.zshrc`.** `nvm`, `node`, `npm` and `npx` are stubs that load nvm on first use. `compinit -C` skips the check unless the dump is a day old. The Homebrew paths and `fpath` entry are fixed exports.

**Trade-offs.** The first `node` in each shell takes roughly 90 ms longer (measured), and a newly installed tool's completions can lag until you remove `~/.zcompdump`. I checked PATH, `fpath` and the registered completions for `gh`, `uv` and `git`. I did not test a fresh machine without the cache.

Codex session in /Users/jules/code/pinch (feat/strip-ansi)

USER: pinch should strip ANSI color codes before it trims, colored tracebacks from pytest and rich don't match the trimming regex. add a --keep-color flag to turn that off

ASSISTANT: I'll start with how text flows through the CLI and what the trim code expects.

TOOL exec_command: sed -n 1,40p pinch/trim.py; sed -n 28,50p pinch/cli.py

RESULT: import re

FRAME = r'  File "[^\n]*", line \d+(?:, in [^\n]*)?\n(?:    [^\n]*\n)*'
TRACEBACK = re.compile(
    r"Traceback \(most recent call last\):\n"
    r"(?P<frames>(?:" + FRAME + r")+)"
    r"(?P<error>\S[^\n]*)"
)

ASSISTANT: The flow is read, redact, trim. The first pattern line begins with `Traceback`, so a color code before it is harmless, but a color code at the start of each `File` line breaks the two-space indent the pattern needs, because the escape sequence comes first. Rich and pytest both color the `File` lines. I'll confirm with a real sample.

TOOL exec_command: printf 'Traceback (most recent call last):\n\033[2m  File "/app/a.py", line 3, in f\033[0m\n    f()\n\033[31mKeyError\033[0m: x\n' > /tmp/color.txt; uv run python - <<'PY'
from pinch.trim import TRACEBACK
text = open("/tmp/color.txt").read()
print("match:", bool(TRACEBACK.search(text)))
PY

RESULT: match: False

ASSISTANT: Confirmed. Now the stripping function. ANSI escape sequences have two common families: CSI sequences, which start with `ESC [` and cover colors and cursor moves, and OSC sequences, which start with `ESC ]` and are used for hyperlinks and window titles. Terminal tools like `ls` and `rich` emit OSC 8 hyperlinks, so stripping only CSI would leave visible junk. I'll handle both.

*** Update File: pinch/trim.py
@@
 import re

+CSI = r"\x1b\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]"
+OSC = r"\x1b\][^\x07\x1b]*(?:\x07|\x1b\\)"
+ANSI = re.compile(f"{CSI}|{OSC}")
+
+
+def strip_ansi(text: str) -> str:
+    return ANSI.sub("", text)
+
 FRAME = r'  File "[^\n]*", line \d+(?:, in [^\n]*)?\ …

# Weeknight dal

Red lentils, one pot, about thirty minutes.

- 1 cup red lentils, rinsed
- 3 cups water
- 1 onion, 3 cloves garlic, thumb of ginger
- 1 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp garam masala
- 1 can diced tomatoes
- Lemon, cilantro

Toast the cumin in oil, then onion, garlic and ginger. Add lentils, water, turmeric, tomatoes. Simmer until it falls apart. Finish with garam masala and lemon.

Good over rice or just with a spoon.

title: Forward recorded headers on replay, add --stripe-secret
content:
Claude Code session in /Users/jules/code/hookbox (replay-headers)

USER: hookbox issue 41. replay drops Stripe-Signature because we only forward content-type and user-agent. forward all recorded headers except host and content-length. also add --stripe-secret that re-signs stripe events with a fresh timestamp so old events pass the 5 minute tolerance

TOOL Grep: ALLOWED_HEADERS in /Users/jules/code/hookbox/src

RESULT: /Users/jules/code/hookbox/src/hookbox/replay.py:9:ALLOWED_HEADERS = ("content-type", "user-agent")
/Users/jules/code/hookbox/src/hookbox/replay.py:31:    headers = {k: v for k, v in event.headers.items() if k.lower() in ALLOWED_HEADERS}

TOOL Read: /Users/jules/code/hookbox/src/hookbox/replay.py

RESULT: import httpx

from hookbox.store import Event

ALLOWED_HEADERS = ("content-type", "user-agent")


def replay(event: Event, target: str, timeout: float = 10.0) -> httpx.Response:
    headers = {k: v for k, v in event.headers.items() if k.lower() in ALLOWED_HEADERS}
    return httpx.post(target, conte …

ASSISTANT: Two changes in `replay.py`:

1. Swap the allowlist for a small denylist. `Host` has to go because the target differs from the original, and `Content-Length` because httpx computes it from the body. I'll also drop hop-by-hop headers (`Connection`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Keep-Alive`), which describe the original connection, not the request.
2. `--stripe-secret`: Stripe's header reads `t=<unix time>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "t.body">`. With a secret, I'll compute a new `t` from the current time and a new `v1`, and replace the header. Without the flag, the recorded header is sent as is, so a replay within 5 minutes of capture still verifies with the original signature.

The body has to be sent byte for byte as recorded, which it already is (`content=event.body`).

title: [default/telegram] Pothos with yellow leaves
content:
Hermes telegram session, profile default, Jules Marlow

USER: my pothos has a few yellow leaves on the bottom. dying?

ASSISTANT: Probably not. A couple of yellow leaves near the base is often normal aging, because the plant drops its oldest leaves. Check these before worrying:

- Soil. Push a finger in about two inches. If it is still wet, you are overwatering, which is the most common cause. Let it dry out between waterings.
- Drainage. Make sure the pot has a hole and the plant is not sitting in a saucer of water.
- Light. Very dim spots can yellow leaves too.

If many leaves are yellow, the stems are mushy, or the soil smells sour, that points to root rot and it is worth taking it out of the pot to look at the roots. Healthy roots are white or tan and firm.

USER: soil is pretty wet still

ASSISTANT: Then hold off on water for now. Wait until the top two inches are dry, which could take a week or more depending on light. Pothos forgive drying out far better than staying wet.

title: Quiet Workflow 213: When the automation breaks at 2 a.m.
content:
From: Quiet Workflow <weekly@quietworkflow.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-09T12:30:01Z

QUIET WORKFLOW
Issue 213

Hi,

Every automation fails eventually. The ones that hurt are the ones that fail quietly. This week: how to find out before your customers do.

1. A HEARTBEAT, NOT A HOPE

If a job should run every hour, have it write a timestamp somewhere (a cell, a file, a tiny status page). Then have a second, separate check that complains when the timestamp is more than two hours old. The second check is the one that saves you, because a dead job cannot report its own death.

2. A DEAD-LETTER TAB

When a row cannot be processed, do not skip it and do not crash. Move it to a tab called "needs a human" with the error message beside it. A florist we spoke to lost six orders over a month because her script quietly dropped any row with a blank delivery field. A dead-letter tab would have shown all six on day one.

3. MAKE REPLAYS SAFE

Sooner or later you will run the same batch twice. Give every record a stable ID (order number plus source, for example) and check for it before you write. If running the job twice gives the same result as running it once, you can retry without fear.

4. ONE LOUD ALERT BEATS TEN QUIET ONES

Alert fatigue is real. Pick one channel (a text, a Slack message to yourself), send only failures, and include what failed and what to do. "Order sync failed: 3 rows in needs-a-human, see sheet" is useful. "Error 500" is not.

READER CORNER

Rosalind from a bike repair shop in Ohio shared her checklist for new automations: who gets told when it fails, where the raw input lives, how to turn it off. Three lines. We printed it. https://quietworkflow.example/community/three-line-checklist

Tobias

title: [default/telegram] Tire pressure for 700x28
content:

USER: what psi for 700x28 tires on a road bike, i weigh about 75 kg

TOOL web_search: 700x28 tire pressure chart rider weight 75 kg tubed

RESULT: For 28 mm tires, typical guidance for a ~75 kg rider is roughly 75-85 psi front and 80-90 psi rear with tubes; lower with tubeless. Always stay under the maximum printed on the sidewall.

ASSISTANT: With tubes, a reasonable starting point is around 80 psi front and 85 psi rear. The usual range for 28 mm tires at your weight is 75 to 90 psi.

A few notes:
- The rear carries more weight, so it gets a bit more.
- Tubeless setups run lower, roughly 10 to 15 psi less, because there is no tube to pinch.
- Never go above the maximum printed on the sidewall of the tire.
- Rough roads or rain call for a little less. Hard, smooth pavement can take a little more.

If the ride feels harsh, drop 5 psi at a time until it feels good and the tire does not squirm in corners.

title: jules-marlow/hookbox#41 [issue closed]: Replayed Stripe events fail signature verification
content:
issue closed | author kallweit-j | created 2026-09-04T16:12:01Z | closed 2026-09-09T20:20:23Z | labels bug

hookbox 0.8.0, Python 3.12, macOS.

I record Stripe test events with `hookbox serve` and replay them into my Flask app:

```
hookbox replay 118 --to http://localhost:5000/stripe/webhook
```

The app answers 400 with `No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload`. The original delivery
from Stripe passed. Comparing the two requests in my app's log, the replayed one has no `Stripe-Signature` header at
all.

---

jules-marlow (2026-09-04T19:05:25Z): Confirmed, thanks for the clear report. `replay` only forwards `Content-Type` and
`User-Agent`. That allowlist dates from 0.3, when I only cared about JSON bodies. The fix is to forward every
recorded header except `Host` and `Content-Length`, which the client sets itself.

That alone won't fix old events, though: Stripe's signature includes a timestamp and the libraries reject anything
older than 5 minutes by default. I'll add a flag that re-signs the payload with a fresh timestamp using your
endpoint secret.

---

kallweit-j (2026-09-04T20:30:53Z): Re-signing would be great, I usually replay events from days ago.

---

jules-marlow (2026-09-09T20:20:22Z): Released in 0.8.1. `replay` now forwards the recorded headers, and
`hookbox replay 118 --to ... --stripe-secret whsec_...` re-signs the event with the current time so old events pass
verification. Closing, reopen if it misbehaves.

title: Walrus Digest #302: background tasks vs a queue, zoneinfo, OCR on scans
content:
From: Walrus Digest <editor@walrusdigest.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-10T13:00:42Z

WALRUS DIGEST
Issue 302

Morning,

1. FASTAPI BACKGROUND TASKS VS A REAL QUEUE

Background tasks are great for "send the email after you return the response." They are risky for anything you cannot afford to lose, because they live and die with the worker process. A deploy in the middle of a task drops the task. The post draws the line clearly: if a lost job means a lost customer order, use a queue (even a database table with a status column and a polling worker). If a lost job means a missed analytics ping, background tasks are fine. https://walrusdigest.example/links/background-vs-queue

2. ZONEINFO AND THE HOUR THAT DOES NOT EXIST

A walk through the standard library's zoneinfo, with a focus on the two bad hours a year: the one that doesn't exist in spring and the one that happens twice in fall. Includes a test helper that freezes time on both transitions. If you store local times without a zone, you will learn this lesson the hard way. https://walrusdigest.example/links/zoneinfo-dst

3. TESSERACT ON SCANNED INVOICES

Practical settings for getting usable text from low-quality scans: binarize and deskew first, set the page segmentation mode to match the layout, and restrict the character set when you know a field is digits only. The author also recommends cropping the invoice number region and OCR-ing it on its own. Accuracy on that field jumped. https://walrusdigest.example/links/tesseract-scans

RELEASES WORTH NOTICING

- A new minor release of Ruff adds rules around implicit string concatenation in collections.
- pytest's latest release tightens how it reports fixture teardown errors.
- A popular HTTP client library deprecated a long-standing retry argument.

SHORT TAKES

- Don't parse dates with a hand-written regex. Use a parser, then test it against your ugliest real input.
- `subprocess.run(..., check=True)` is a gift. Use it.
- Logging the full request body? Redact before you write it down.

Until next week,
The Walrus Digest team

1. **Honeypot.** A field humans never see or fill. Bots that fill every input reveal themselves.
2. **Time to submit.** A render timestamp in a hidden field. A form filled in under three seconds is a script.
3. **Link count.** SEO pitches carry URLs and real inquiries rarely carry more than one or two.
4. **Rate limit per address.** A backstop for anything that gets through.

For rejected submissions I'd answer with the same redirect a real submission gets. A visible error tells a bot author what to change. I'll put the rules in a pure function in `src/lib/contact.ts` so they can be unit tested without a server.

title: The Backhaul: Freight audit season, where invoice errors hide
content:
From: The Backhaul <desk@backhaulbrief.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-11T12:00:11Z

THE BACKHAUL
Vol. 9, No. 34

FREIGHT AUDIT SEASON: WHERE INVOICE ERRORS HIDE

With fourth-quarter budgets being set, shippers are taking a harder look at what they paid carriers in the first three quarters. Auditors we spoke to say a typical mid-size shipper overpays between one and three percent on freight invoices, mostly through errors that are tedious rather than clever.

The top five, in the order auditors say they find them:

1. Duplicate invoices, usually the same load billed once by the carrier and again after a rebill.
2. Accessorial charges (liftgate, residential delivery, detention) with no supporting proof of delivery.
3. Fuel surcharge calculated on the wrong index week.
4. Rate drift, where the invoiced linehaul does not match the contracted lane rate.
5. Weight or class corrections applied after the fact with no reweigh ticket.

THE DOCUMENT PROBLEM

Almost every audit stalls on the same thing. The invoice is a PDF, the bill of lading is a different PDF, the rate confirmation is an email, and the TMS record holds a fourth version. Someone has to line up four sources by hand. A logistics manager at a Texas shipper told us her team spends about two days a month on exactly this.

Software vendors are circling the problem. Most pitches combine OCR with field extraction and a match against the TMS. The ones that survive a pilot tend to do one boring thing well, such as pulling the load number, carrier name, invoice total and ship date into a clean row, and flagging what they could not read.

NUMBERS TO KNOW

- Average days to pay a carrier invoice (reported): 38
- Share of invoices needing one or more corrections: 14 percent
- Share of audits that found duplicate payments: 41 percent

Webinar next Thursday: 'Matching invoices to rate confirmations without losing your mind.' https://backhaulbrief.example/events/matching-webinar

The Backhaul desk

title: Client onboarding checklist
content:
notes/Areas/Business

---
tags: [business, template]
---
# Client onboarding checklist

A template. Copy into the client note and tick as you go.

## Before the first call
- [ ] Read whatever they sent
- [ ] Write down what I think the problem is, in one sentence

## First call
- [ ] Who decides, who uses it, who pays
- [ ] What "done" looks like
- [ ] What they do today, step by step
- [ ] What goes wrong most often

## Access and data
- [ ] Sample of real data (with their say-so)
- [ ] Accounts and permissions, written down
- [ ] Where to send questions

## Ground rules
- [ ] How change requests arrive
- [ ] Who to call if it breaks
- [ ] Where the code and docs live

## After
- [ ] Short recap email the same day
- [ ] Add to [[Weekly review]]

## Red flags worth noticing early
- Nobody can say who decides.
- The data lives only in one person's head.
- Everything is urgent, all the time.
- "It should be simple" with no example attached.

## Tone
Plain words, no jargon, one question at a time. People tell you more when they are not being quizzed.

title: Add git aliases for a short log and cleaning merged branches
content:
Claude Code session in /Users/jules/code/dotfiles (main)

USER: add a few git aliases to the dotfiles. a pretty one-line log with graph, a status that's short, and one that deletes local branches that are already merged into main. be careful with the delete one

ASSISTANT: The delete alias is the dangerous one, so I'll design it to be conservative and then test it on a throwaway repository. First I'll find where the git config lives in the dotfiles repo.

TOOL Bash: ls git git/.config/git; sed -n 1,30p git/.config/git/config

RESULT: .config
config  ignore
[user]
	name = Jules Marlow
	email = jules@marlowworks.dev
[init]
	defaultBranch = main
[pull]
	rebase = true
[alias]
	co = checkout

ASSISTANT: There is an `[alias]` section already with one entry. I'll add the new aliases there. For the cleanup alias these are the rules I want. It must list only branches fully merged into `main`, using `git branch --merged main`, which lists branches whose tip is reachable from main, so unmerged work is never touched. It must skip `main` itself and the current branch, whose line starts with `*`. And it must delete with `-d`, never `-D`, so git refuses anything it considers unmerged even if my filter were wrong.

TOOL Edit: /Users/jules/code/dotfiles/git/.config/git/config
old: 	co = checkout
new: 	co = checkout
	st = status -sb
	lg = log --graph --abbrev-commit --decorate --date=relative --format=format:'%C(bold blue)%h%C(reset) %C(green)(%ar)%C(reset) %s %C(dim white)- %an%C(reset)%C(auto)%d%C(reset)'
	cleanup = "!gi …

RESULT: The file /Users/jules/code/dotfiles/git/.config/git/config has been updated.

ASSISTANT: In a git config file, a double-quoted value needs its backslashes doubled, so `\\*` in the file reaches the shell as `\*`. That is easy to get wrong, so let me look at what git thinks the alias is, and not trust my reading of the file.

TOOL Bash: git config --file git/.config/git/config alias.cleanup

RESULT: !git branch --merged main | grep -v -E '^\*|^[[:space:]]*main$' | xargs -r git branch -d

ASSISTANT: The shell sees `'^\*|^[[:space:]]*main$'`, which is what I intended. I used `[[:space:]]` instead of `\s` because the BSD `grep` on macOS does not treat `\s` the same way GNU grep does. Now I'll test on a scratch repository with four branches: one merged and not current, one with unmerged commits, one that is current and merged, and `main`. Only the first should be deleted.

TOOL Bash: rm -rf /tmp/alias-test && git init -q -b main /tmp/alias-test && cd /tmp/alias-test && git config user.email t@mail.example && git config user.name Test && git commit -q --allow-empty -m base \
&& git checkout -q -b feature/merged && git commit -q --allow-empty -m a && git checkout -q main && git me …

RESULT: * feature/current
  feature/merged
  feature/unmerged
  main

TOOL Bash: cd /tmp/alias-test && GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/Users/jules/code/dotfiles/git/.config/git/config git cleanup; echo "exit=$?"; git branch

RESULT: Deleted branch feature/merged (was 1e21709).
exit=0
* feature/current
  feature/unmerged
  main

ASSISTANT: Exactly right. `feature/merged` is gone, `feature/unmerged` survived, and neither the current branch nor `main` was touched. `feature/current` was created from `main` after the merge, so it has no commits of its own and counts as merged. The `*` filter is the only thing that protected it, which is the case I most wanted to test.

One more edge: running it with nothing to delete. `xargs -r` makes it a no-op on empty input. macOS `xargs` ignores `-r` and does not run on empty input anyway, so this works on both.

TOOL Bash: cd /tmp/alias-test && GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/Users/jules/code/dotfiles/git/.config/git/config git cleanup; echo "exit=$?"

RESULT: exit=0

ASSISTANT: Nothing to delete gives a clean exit with no output. Now the log alias, in the same scratch repo with a little history so the graph has something to draw.

TOOL Bash: cd /tmp/alias-test && git checkout -q feature/unmerged && git commit -q --allow-empty -m "second change" && git tag -a v-test -m t && export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/Users/jules/code/dotfiles/git/.config/git/config && git lg -5 --all | cat && echo && git st; cd /tmp && rm -rf /tmp/alias-test

RESULT: * a453c5b (0 seconds ago) second change - Test (HEAD -> feature/unmerged, tag: v-test)
* 0893f6c (0 seconds ago) b - Test
*   d53fdf6 (0 seconds ago) merge - Test (main, feature/current)
|\
| * 1e21709 (0 seconds ago) a - Test
|/
* 1216999 (0 seconds ago) base - Test

## feature/unmerged

USER: good. is lg going to look right in a pager

ASSISTANT: It depends on color handling. `git log` sends output to `less`, and git passes `-R` to `less` by default when `LESS` is not set, so the ANSI color codes render. I'll check what your config sets for the pager, because a custom `core.pager` can drop that.

TOOL Bash: git config --get core.pager; echo "LESS=$LESS"; rg -n "pager" git/.config/git/config zsh/.zshrc

RESULT: (core.pager not set)
LESS=-FRX

ASSISTANT: No custom pager, and `LESS=-FRX` includes `-R`, so colors pass through, and `-F` makes `less` exit immediately when the output fits on one screen. The alias will look right as it is. I'm done with the changes, and I'll commit.

TOOL Bash: git add -A && git commit -qm "git: add st, lg and cleanup aliases" && git log --oneline -1

RESULT: 41c9e08 git: add st, lg and cleanup aliases

ASSISTANT: Committed locally.

**Added to `git/.config/git/config`.** `git st` is `status -sb`. `git lg` is a one-line graph log with relative dates, authors and refs. `git cleanup` deletes local branches already merged into `main`.

**How `cleanup` stays safe.** It lists branches with `--merged main`, skips `main` and the current branch, and deletes with `-d`, so git refuses anything unmerged even if the filter were wrong.

**Checked.** I ran it on a scratch repository with a merged branch, an unmerged branch, the current branch and `main`. Only the merged one was deleted, and a second run with nothing to delete exited cleanly. The pager shows the colors because `LESS` contains `-R`. It only looks at local branches, so branches that were squash-merged on GitHub show as unmerged and stay until you remove them by hand.

# gb [query]: pick a local branch with fzf (newest first) and switch to it.
gb() {
  local branch
  branch=$(
    git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads \
      | fzf --height 40% --reverse --sel …

RESULT: [ -r "$HOME/.config/zsh/git.zsh" ] && source "$HOME/.config/zsh/git.zsh"

hotfix/login

feature/old
main

RESULT: Switched to branch 'hotfix/login'
hotfix/login

ASSISTANT: The query `hotfix` matched exactly one branch, so the function switched without showing a menu. The next two cases are zero matches, which should exit quietly and leave the branch alone, and several matches, where fzf would normally open a menu. I can't drive a menu from a script, but I can check that a multi-match query does not auto-select.

TOOL exec_command: cd /tmp/gb-test && git switch -q main && zsh -f -c 'source /Users/jules/code/dotfiles/zsh/.config/zsh/git.zsh; gb nonexistent-branch; echo "status=$?"; git branch --show-current'; echo ---; git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads | fzf --filter=feature | head -5

RESULT: status=1
main
---
feature/old
feature/new
feature/mid

ASSISTANT: With no match the function returns without switching, and the branch is still `main`. The status is 1, which is fzf's code for "no match" and passes through, which is fine for an interactive helper. The `--filter=feature` check shows three branches match, so `--select-1` would not fire and fzf would open the menu there, as intended. I'll clean up and commit.

## main

ASSISTANT: `gb` is in `zsh/.config/zsh/git.zsh`, sourced from `.zshrc` when the file exists. title: Sourdough loaf
content:
notes/Recipes

---
tags: [recipe, bread]
---
# Sourdough loaf

## Starter
Feed 1:5:5 (starter, flour, water). Use it when it has doubled and just started to dome. If it has collapsed, it is late.

## Dough
- 500 g bread flour
- 350 g water
- 100 g active starter
- 10 g salt

## Method
1. Mix flour and water, rest 30 minutes (autolyse).
2. Add starter and salt. Fold every 30 minutes, four times.
3. Bulk until about 50 percent bigger. Shape. Fridge overnight.
4. Bake in a preheated Dutch oven, lid on, then lid off to finish.

## Notes
- Hydration is the lever. Too wet and the loaf spreads, too dry and it's dense.
- Underfed starter makes a brick. Learned that the hard way.

## Troubleshooting
- Dense crumb: starter was late or bulk was short.
- Gummy middle: cut it too soon. Wait an hour.
- Flat loaf: dough was too slack, add a fold or two next time.
- Pale crust: bake the second half with the lid off a little longer.

title: [default/telegram] Summary of a pasted trucking article
content:
Hermes telegram session, profile default, Jules Marlow

USER: summarize this for me, 3 bullets max

Short-haul carriers brace for a slow fall season

Regional trucking companies say demand for short-haul routes has flattened as retailers trim their inventory ahead of the holidays. Several mid-sized fleets told Haulwise Daily that spot rates for runs under 250 miles have slipped for a third month, while contract rates have held steady.

Analysts point to two causes. First, shippers who stocked up early in the summer now have full warehouses, so they are booking fewer extra loads. Second, a wave of small carriers that entered the market last year added capacity, which pushes rates down.

Fleet owners are responding in different ways. Some are parking older trucks rather than cutting driver pay. Others are shifting trucks to dedicated contract lanes, which pay less per mile but run predictably. A few are pausing orders for new equipment until the picture clears.

Industry groups expect the slowdown to ease once holiday shipping ramps up, though they caution that new capacity may keep rates soft into the new year.

ASSISTANT: - Demand for short-haul trucking has flattened as retailers cut inventory ahead of the holidays. Spot rates on runs under 250 miles have fallen for three months, while contract rates are steady.
- The article blames early summer stockpiling by shippers and extra capacity from many new small carriers.
- Fleets are parking older trucks, moving to contract lanes, or pausing equipment orders. Industry groups expect relief when holiday shipping picks up, but say extra capacity may keep rates soft into the new year.

USER: whats a spot rate

ASSISTANT: A spot rate is the price for a single load booked right now, at the going market price. A contract rate is a price agreed in advance for a set period, usually for regular loads on a lane. Spot rates move with daily supply and demand, and contract rates move slowly.

THE PROOFING DRAWER
For independent bakeries | Fall menu issue

FALL MENU PLANNING: APPLE, PEAR, AND THE PUMPKIN QUESTION

Every September, bakeries split into two camps. One has been selling pumpkin since the 1st. The other refuses to touch it until the first cold morning. The data, from a poll of 212 shops: 58 percent launched a pumpkin item before the autumn equinox, and shops that did saw a 9 percent lift in morning sales for the first three weeks, then a plateau.

THE SHORT LIST THAT SELLS

- Apple: hand pies, cider-glazed donuts, galettes. Shops that rotated the apple variety weekly got repeat visits.
- Pear: ginger-pear scones outsold plain pear tarts two to one at three shops.
- Squash: savory focaccia with roasted squash and sage is the sleeper hit of the season.
- Spiced anything: chai and cardamom are easier to run than pumpkin pie spice, and customers think they are fancier.

MENU CARD TIPS

Rye Street Bakehouse in Duluth prints its menu card weekly and writes only the items that are guaranteed. A chalkboard "ask us" line holds the experiments. Their sold-out rate dropped, and so did staff stress at the counter.

SUPPLY WATCH

Butter prices are up about 6 percent over last year, with cultured butter up more. Flour contracts for the holiday season are being signed now. A mill in Kansas is offering fixed pricing through January to shops that commit by month's end.

Next week: pre-orders without the chaos.

title: [default/telegram] Books about how software teams ship
content:
Hermes telegram session, profile default, Jules Marlow

USER: just finished a book about how teams ship software and loved it. what else is like that

ASSISTANT: Some that fit, from older classics to newer:

1. The Soul of a New Machine. A narrative account of a team racing to build a computer. Reads like a novel.
2. Peopleware. Short chapters on why teams succeed or fail, mostly about people and not tools.
3. The Mythical Man-Month. Essays on why adding people to a late project makes it later. Dated in places but the core ideas hold.
4. Accelerate. Research on which practices predict a team that ships well, with numbers.

If you liked a story-style book, start with the first. If you liked practical lessons, try the fourth. What was the one you finished?

USER: it was one of the ones about incident reviews

ASSISTANT: Then I would start with Peopleware, since it overlaps the most with how teams handle mistakes, and Accelerate for the measured side. The Soul of a New Machine is the one to read if you want the human drama.

title: Net Thirty #59: Deposits without the awkward
content:
From: Net Thirty <hello@netthirty.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-15T13:02:37Z

NET THIRTY
Issue 59

Hi again,

Last issue was about chasing money. This one is about not having to chase it, which starts before the project does.

1. THE DEPOSIT CONVERSATION

The awkward version: "I require a deposit." The easy version: "To hold a start date, the first payment is due when you sign. Everything after that is billed as we hit milestones."

Said that way, the deposit is a scheduling tool, not a trust test. Several readers told us clients stopped negotiating it once it was attached to a start date instead of to the client's credit.

2. THREE STRUCTURES READERS ACTUALLY USE

- Half up front, half on delivery. Simple, but leaves a long gap on projects over six weeks.
- Thirds: signing, midpoint review, handoff. The midpoint doubles as a forced check-in.
- Monthly in advance for ongoing work, billed on the first so it clears before you do the month's work.

Whichever you pick, put the due date of each payment in the contract as a calendar date or a named event. "Upon completion" is where disputes live.

3. WHEN A COMPANY SAYS THEY ONLY PAY AGAINST A PO

Ask for the PO number before you start, not before you invoice. One reader keeps a line at the top of every statement of work: "Work begins when a PO number or written approval is received." Nobody has objected to it yet.

4. LINKS

- A deposit clause you can paste into a statement of work: https://netthirty.example/templates/deposit
- Cash buffers for irregular income, with a worksheet: https://netthirty.example/guides/buffer
- Reader thread: do you bill expenses at cost? https://netthirty.example/community/expenses-at-cost

See you on the 29th.
Carmen

ASSISTANT: Python prints the oldest call first and the failing call last, which is why pinch keeps frames at both ends. Node and Java print the exception line first and then frames with the newest on top, so the useful frames are at the start and the tail is mostly framework internals. title: Pricing thoughts
content:
notes/Areas/Business

---
tags: [business, pricing]
---
# Pricing thoughts

No numbers here, just ways of thinking.

## Value pricing, in general
- Price follows what the outcome is worth to the buyer, not hours spent.
- A tool that saves a small team a few hours of repetitive work every week has a value that has little to do with how long it took to write.
- The hardest part is learning what the problem costs them now. Ask.

## Questions to ask
- What happens if nothing changes?
- Who feels the pain: the owner, the manager, or the person doing the clicking?
- What would "done" look like in one sentence?

## Things to be careful about
- Fixed fees punish scope creep unless scope is written down.
- Hourly rewards slow work.
- Discounts teach buyers to ask for them. Trading scope is cleaner.

## Framing
- Describe the result first and the work second.
- Offer two or three shapes of the same thing (small, standard, thorough) so the conversation is about scope, not about whether to say yes.
- Say the number plainly, then stop talking.

## What I notice
- The projects people are proudest of are the ones where the owner could say what the problem cost them.
- Vague goals produce vague invoices and vague feelings about them.
- Cheap work attracts the most opinions about how it should be done.

## Open
- When is a retainer better than a project?
- How do you talk about ongoing upkeep without it sounding like a tax?

See [[Client onboarding checklist]].

title: Quiet Workflow 214: The spreadsheet is a fine database (until it isn't)
content:
From: Quiet Workflow <weekly@quietworkflow.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-16T12:30:33Z

QUIET WORKFLOW
Issue 214

Hi,

Whenever we run a piece on spreadsheets someone writes in to say "just use a real database." Sometimes they are right. Here is how to tell.

WHEN GOOGLE SHEETS IS ENOUGH

- A few thousand rows, a handful of editors, and the people who read the data are not developers.
- Your staff already live in it. Adoption is a feature.
- You want a human to be able to fix a bad row with a click and an undo.

SIGNS YOU'RE OUTGROWING IT

1. Quota errors. If your script starts seeing "429 Quota exceeded for quota metric 'Read requests'", you are reading cell by cell. Batch the reads (one call for the whole range) before you decide anything else.
2. Two things write to the same row at once and the last writer wins. This one is subtle and shows up as "sometimes a number is wrong."
3. You have formulas that reference formulas that reference another file. One broken link and half the sheet turns to #REF!.
4. Somebody asks "can we see this by customer over the last two years?" and the answer takes an afternoon.

THE MOVE, WHEN YOU MAKE IT

You do not have to throw the sheet away. A common pattern: keep the sheet as the friendly face for staff, put Postgres underneath for anything that needs history or reporting, and sync one direction. The sheet shows; the database remembers.

LINKS

- Batch reads and writes with the Sheets API: https://quietworkflow.example/tools/sheets-batch
- A reader's migration notes, sheet to Postgres in a weekend: https://quietworkflow.example/community/sheet-to-postgres
- Poll results: how many rows is too many? https://quietworkflow.example/polls/row-count

Tobias

title: The Recall Letter #78: Reminder texts that get replies
content:
From: The Recall Letter <hello@recallletter.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-16T13:40:08Z

THE RECALL LETTER
Issue 78

REMINDER TEXTS THAT GET REPLIES

We collected 31 reminder templates from member practices and read them all in one sitting. A few patterns separate the ones that get answered from the ones that get ignored.

1. THE PRACTICE NAME COMES FIRST. Patients get texts from numbers they do not know. "Lakemont Pediatric Dentistry: Ava's visit is Tuesday" gets read. "Reminder: appointment Tuesday" looks like spam.

2. ONE ASK PER MESSAGE. "Reply 1 to confirm or 2 to reschedule" outperformed templates that offered four options. Practices that offered a phone number as well saw more calls and fewer replies.

3. SAY WHO THE PATIENT IS. Parents get texts for several children. Put the child's first name in the message, or you will field a call that begins "which one?"

4. A SECOND TOUCH BEATS A BETTER FIRST ONE. Practices that sent a short follow-up to anyone who had not replied saw the biggest lift, more than any rewrite of the first message.

5. NEVER GO PAST THREE. Three touches in total was the ceiling before opt-outs climbed.

WHEN A PATIENT TEXTS BACK SOMETHING ODD

Sandpiper Orthodontics logged a month of replies. About 8 percent were not "yes" or "no": questions about parking, cost, whether a parent could bring a sibling, "wrong number." Their front desk now checks the reply inbox before each opening and again before close. Unanswered replies were the main source of one-star reviews.

TEMPLATE LIBRARY (members): https://recallletter.example/templates/reminders
Next webinar: Handling the angry no-show call. https://recallletter.example/webinars/angry-no-show

The Recall Letter team

content:
Codex session in /Users/jules/code/fernbrook-orders (chore/ruff-rules)

USER: tighten ruff in fernbrook-orders: add I, UP and B rules and fix what they find. add pre-commit with the ruff hooks and a hook that fails if uv.lock is stale

ASSISTANT: I'll look at the current ruff config and the dev dependencies.

TOOL exec_command: grep -n "ruff" -A4 pyproject.toml; cat .github/workflows/ci.yml | tail -6

RESULT: [tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
dev = ["pytest>=8.3", "ruff>=0.8"]
      - run: uv run ruff check .
      - run: uv run ruff format --check .
      - run: uv run pytest -q

ASSISTANT: Ruff has only a line length, so it runs with its default rules, which are a small set of pycodestyle and pyflakes checks. CI already runs the check and the format check. I'll add the rule selection and see what turns up before changing any code.

TOOL exec_command: cat >> pyproject.toml <<'TOML'

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B"]
TOML
uv run ruff check . 2>&1 | tail -14

ERROR: src/fernbrook_orders/app.py:21:36: B008 Do not perform function call `Form` in argument defaults; instead, perform the call within the function, or read the default from a module-level singleton variable
src/fernbrook_orders/app.py:21:67: B008 Do not perform function call `Form` in argument defaults; instead, perform the call within the function, or read the default from a module-level singleton variable
src/fernbrook_orders/sheets.py:3:1: UP035 [*] Import from `collections.abc` instead: `Iterable`
src/fernbrook_orders/sheets.py:5:1: I001 [*] Import block is un-sorted or un-formatted
tests/test_sheets.py:2:1: I001 [*] Import block is un-sorted or un-formatted
Found 5 errors.
[*] 3 fixable with the `--fix` option.

ASSISTANT: Five findings, three auto-fixable. The two `B008` hits are in the webhook handler, where `Form(...)` appears in parameter defaults. That is how FastAPI declares request parameters, so this is a well-known false positive and not a bug. Rewriting to avoid it would fight the framework. Ruff has a setting for this: the bugbear plugin accepts a list of calls that are safe to use as defaults.

TOOL exec_command: cat >> pyproject.toml <<'TOML'

[tool.ruff.lint.flake8-bugbear]
extend-immutable-calls = ["fastapi.Form", "fastapi.Query", "fastapi.Depends"]
TOML
uv run ruff check --fix . 2>&1 | tail -4; git diff --stat | tail -4

RESULT: Found 3 errors (3 fixed, 0 remaining).
 pyproject.toml                  | 6 ++++++
 src/fernbrook_orders/sheets.py  | 5 +++--
 tests/test_sheets.py            | 3 ++-
 3 files changed, 11 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)

ASSISTANT: Lint is clean. I allowed `Form`, `Query` and `Depends` and not only `Form`, because the next route that uses a query parameter or a dependency would hit the same false positive. Next I'll confirm the format check and tests still pass after the auto-fixes, then write the pre-commit config.

TOOL exec_command: uv run ruff format --check . 2>&1 | tail -2; uv run pytest -q 2>&1 | tail -2

RESULT: 20 files already formatted
..............                                                         [100%]
14 passed in 0.50s

TOOL exec_command: cat > .pre-commit-config.yaml <<'EOF'
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: v0.13.0
    hooks:
      - id: ruff-check
        args: [--fix]
      - id: ruff-format
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv-pre-commit
    rev: 0.8.17
    hooks:
      - id: uv-lock
  - …

RESULT: + pre-commit==4.3.0
pre-commit installed at .git/hooks/pre-commit
ruff check...............................................................Passed
ruff format..............................................................Passed
uv-lock..................................................................P …

ASSISTANT: Every hook passes on the current tree. I'll commit in two steps first, the code fixes and then the tooling, so the working tree is clean before I test anything destructive.

TOOL exec_command: git add src tests && git commit -qm "Apply ruff I and UP fixes" && git add -A && git commit -qm "Enable ruff I, UP, B; add pre-commit with ruff and uv-lock hooks" 2>&1 | tail -3; git log --oneline -2; git status --short | wc -l

RESULT: uv-lock..................................................................Passed
8c1d0e9 Enable ruff I, UP, B; add pre-commit with ruff and uv-lock hooks
4a77f20 Apply ruff I and UP fixes
0

ASSISTANT: Both commits went through the hooks, and the tree is clean. A hook that has never failed is not proven, so I'll check the `uv-lock` hook where it matters: change a dependency in `pyproject.toml` without updating the lock, stage it, and try to commit.

TOOL exec_command: sed -i '' 's/dependencies = \["fastapi", /dependencies = ["fastapi", "orjson", /' pyproject.toml && git add pyproject.toml && git commit -qm "scratch: dependency without lock" 2>&1 | tail -6; git status --short

ERROR: uv-lock..................................................................Failed
- hook id: uv-lock
- files were modified by this hook
Resolved 33 packages in 214ms
Added orjson v3.11.3
 M uv.lock
M  pyproject.toml

ASSISTANT: The hook refused the commit and rewrote `uv.lock` to include `orjson`, so it catches a stale lock and fixes it, leaving the change for me to stage. The commit did not happen. Everything before the scratch edit is committed, so restoring the two files loses nothing.

TOOL exec_command: git restore --staged --worktree pyproject.toml uv.lock; git status --short | wc -l; grep -c orjson pyproject.toml uv.lock; git log --oneline -1

RESULT: 0
pyproject.toml:0
uv.lock:0
8c1d0e9 Enable ruff I, UP, B; add pre-commit with ruff and uv-lock hooks

ASSISTANT: Ruff now selects `E`, `F`, `I`, `UP` and `B` in `pyproject.toml`. It found five issues. The three fixable ones, an import order in two files and a `collections.abc` import, are fixed in their own commit. The two `B008` hits were `Form(...)` in the webhook parameters, a known false positive with FastAPI, so the config allows `Form`, `Query` and `Depends` as immutable calls. `.pre-commit-config.yaml` runs ruff check and format, the `uv-lock` hook, and three file hygiene hooks. I tested the lock hook by adding a dependency without locking: it blocked the commit and rewrote `uv.lock`, and I restored both files afterwards. The final state passes lint, format, 14 tests and all hooks. I have not run the workflow on GitHub.

- Why SMS reminders need a stop word
- What a nightly CSV export taught me about other people's software
- OCR on messy PDFs: the stuff the tutorials skip
- A webhook handler that survives retries
- Small automations I would skip building
- Reading carrier invoices at scale, without the scale

## Pitches, in a sentence each
- Pocket log trimmer: nobody wants to paste 4,000 lines of stack trace into a chat, and nobody wants to paste a secret either.
- Stop word: the smallest reply a reminder text can handle, and why you want it from day one.
- CSV export: it is a contract, even if nobody wrote it down.

## Format thoughts
- Short. Under 900 words.
- One code block that actually runs.
- End with what I would do differently.

Rank them after a week. Anything that still sounds good then goes on the site.

1. TYPEDDICT, DATACLASS, PYDANTIC: WHERE EACH GOES

A clear framework from a conference talk transcript. TypedDict describes dictionaries you do not control (JSON in, JSON out). Dataclasses are for plain values inside your code. Pydantic belongs at the edge, where untrusted input becomes trusted data, because validation is the whole point. Developers paste logs into chat tools and bug trackers all day. A short guide on stripping secrets, emails, IP addresses and tokens first, with a comparison of regex-based and entropy-based approaches. title: The Quiet Machinery
author: Edda Rowan
type: book
status: finished
tags: [reading, nonfiction, history]

# The Quiet Machinery

A history of automatic looms and the people who worked beside them. Sounds dry. Isn't.

## What stuck
- Every big change in the mill started as a small fix to one annoying step.
- The operators who understood how the machine failed were worth more than the machine.
- Nobody noticed the loom was "automatic" until it stopped. Same with most software.

## Quote
> A machine that never fails teaches no one anything about itself.

## To think about
- Upkeep as invisible work. Could be a post, see [[Blog post ideas]].
- The chapter on the night shift reads like an on-call story.

title: The Backhaul: The paperwork gap between brokers and carriers
content:
From: The Backhaul <desk@backhaulbrief.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-18T12:00:50Z

THE BACKHAUL
Vol. 9, No. 35

THE PAPERWORK GAP BETWEEN BROKERS AND CARRIERS

Ask a small carrier what slows its cash flow and the answer is rarely rates. It is paperwork. Ask a broker the same question and you hear the mirror image: carriers send documents in whatever form they have, and every load becomes a small data entry project.

WHAT BROKERS WANT IN THE PACKET

- Signed bill of lading, legible, with the receiver's stamp
- Invoice with the broker's load number, not just the carrier's own
- Lumper or scale receipts when charges are claimed
- Proof of delivery with a time

A broker survey found 22 percent of packets arrive missing at least one of the four, and each incomplete packet adds about six days to payment.

EDI VS PDF

Large carriers send electronic invoices (EDI 210) that drop straight into a payables system. Everyone else sends PDFs. The industry expected PDFs to fade out by now. They have not, and several vendors have pivoted from "replace the PDF" to "read the PDF," extracting fields into the CSV or API format the receiving system wants.

TMS NEWS

A midmarket TMS vendor announced a new document inbox that auto-matches uploaded invoices to open loads. Early adopters say it works well when load numbers are printed clearly and badly when they are handwritten. The vendor says handwriting support is coming.

MERGERS

Redfern Freight closed its purchase of Alder & Cole Logistics. Tamarack Line Haul says it will keep operating its regional fleet under its own name.

The Backhaul desk

Claude Code session in /Users/jules/code/fernbrook-orders (feat/structlog)

USER: add structured logging to fernbrook-orders. json lines on stdout, a request id on every line, use structlog. dont log message bodies

ASSISTANT: I'll see how logging works now, so I know what to replace.

TOOL Bash: rg -n "logging|logger|print\(" src | head -20

RESULT: src/fernbrook_orders/app.py:9:logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

src/fernbrook_orders/app.py:31:    logger.info(f"webhook received ({len(body)} chars)")
src/fernbrook_orders/sheets.py:18:    logger.info(f"appended row {row_numb …

ASSISTANT: The project uses the standard library `logging` with f-strings. Structured logging wants an event name plus separate key-value fields, so each message gets rewritten to that shape, and I'll avoid putting values inside the message text. Your rule about bodies is already respected here, since line 31 logs only a length, and I'll keep it that way.

The design has three parts. A `logging_setup.py` module with `configure_logging(level)` that sets up `structlog` and routes standard library records through the same JSON renderer, so uvicorn and library logs match. A middleware that binds a request id, the method and the path into context variables, so every line inside a request carries them without passing a logger around. And the call sites rewritten to events.

The first got a generated one, the second kept the `abc123` I sent, and `duration_ms` is there. Now a test, so the format does not regress. Structlog has `capture_logs()` for this.

TOOL Bash: cat > tests/test_logging.py <<'PY'
from structlog.testing import capture_logs


def test_request_log_has_context(client):

        client.get("/health", headers={"x-request-id": "req-1"})
    request_logs = [entry for entry in logs if entry["event"] == "request"]

ASSISTANT: In the full run `capture_logs` returns no `request` entry, although the request clearly ran. This is the `cache_logger_on_first_use=True` setting in my configuration. With it on, structlog binds each logger to its processor chain the first time it is used and never looks again. `capture_logs` works by swapping the processors for a moment, so a logger already used by an earlier test, here `test_health`, keeps the old JSON chain and the capture sees nothing. Run alone, the first use happened inside the capture, which is why it passed. I'll remove the setting, since it defaults to off.
